draft.title: Wartime government controls
card: Rationing
The government limited how much food and clothing each person could buy, using coupons. Tea, butter, meat and clothing were rationed so supplies could go to the war effort.
Manpower
The government could direct people into war work, such as factories, farms and mines. This kept important industries running while many men were in the forces.
Censorship
The government controlled what newspapers and radio could report. News that might help the enemy or hurt morale could be cut or banned.
Internment
People seen as enemy aliens, such as some Germans, Italians and Japanese living in Australia, were held in camps. Many had done nothing wrong.
draft.remember: In wartime the government used its power to limit what people bought, where they worked, what they read and where they lived.

a.q: In 1942 a newspaper in Adelaide is told it cannot print a report on a bombing raid. Which wartime control is this?
opts: Censorship of news
Rationing of supplies
Direction into war work
Internment of enemy aliens
a.why: The government decided what the paper could report, which is censorship. It is not rationing, because no goods were limited, and nobody was sent to a camp or a job.
a.clue: Think about who decided what could be printed.

b.q: Rosa, born in Italy, has lived in Fremantle for twenty years and is taken to a camp in 1940, though she has broken no law. Why was she held?
opts: She was seen as an enemy alien because of her origins
She refused to carry out the work she was directed to do
She broke the rules on buying rationed goods
She printed news the government had banned
b.why: Internment targeted people seen as enemy aliens, often because of their birthplace, even when they had done nothing wrong. Rosa broke no law, so the options about work, rationing or banned news do not fit.
b.clue: The card says many held had done nothing wrong.

b.best: She was seen as an enemy alien because of her origins

proposal.title: Wartime government controls
card: Rationing
The government limited how much food and clothing each person could buy, using coupons. Tea, butter, meat and clothing were rationed so supplies could go to the war effort.

The government could direct people into war work, such as factories, farms and mines. This kept important industries running while many men were in the forces.
Censorship
The government controlled what newspapers and radio could report. News that might help the enemy or hurt morale could be cut or banned.
Internment

People seen as enemy aliens, such as some Germans, Italians and Japanese living in Australia, were held in camps. Most were held without trial, because of their background rather than anything they had done.

a.q: In 1942 a newspaper in Adelaide is told it cannot print a report on a bombing raid. Which wartime control is this?
opts: Censorship of news
Rationing of supplies
Direction into war work
Internment of enemy aliens
a.why: The government decided what the paper could report, which is censorship. It is not rationing, because no goods were limited, and nobody was sent to a camp or a job.

b.q: Marco, born in Italy, has lived in Fremantle for twenty years. In 1940, after Italy enters the war, he is taken to a camp. Why was he most likely held?
opts: He was seen as an enemy alien because of his birthplace
He was found guilty in a trial of spying for Italy
He refused to do the war work he was directed to do
He was called up and sent to an army training camp
b.why: Internment held people seen as enemy aliens because of their background, usually without any trial. A court conviction for spying is tempting, but internment was not a punishment decided by a court, and refusing directed work or army call-up are different wartime controls.
b.clue: Was he held for what he did or for where he came from?
